Lack of Time and Procrastination in University Life

Lack of Time and Procrastination
in University Life

In university life, time often feels like a river that runs faster than students expect. Every morning, many students wake up with a long list of responsibilities: classes to attend, assignments to complete, books to read, exams to prepare for, messages to answer, and sometimes even jobs or family duties to manage. At first, everything seems possible.

A student may think, “I still have enough time. I can do it later.” However, that simple sentence can become the beginning of a difficult cycle called procrastination.

Procrastination is not always laziness. Sometimes, students put off their tasks because they feel tired, confused, afraid, or overwhelmed. For example, a student may receive a research assignment and immediately feel that it is too complicated. Instead of starting with a small step, the student avoids it.

They check social media, watch videos, clean their room, talk to friends, or convince themselves that they work better under pressure. Hours pass, then days pass, and the assignment remains untouched.

The lack of time in university is also connected to poor planning. Many students underestimate how much time they need to complete academic tasks. Reading ten pages may look easy, but understanding, taking notes, and preparing a summary can take much longer.

Writing an essay may seem simple, but searching for information, organizing ideas, correcting grammar, and reviewing the final version require patience and discipline. When students do not plan realistically, they often end up working late at night, feeling anxious and exhausted.

There was a student named Leo who always believed he had everything under control. He was intelligent, friendly, and creative, but he had a dangerous habit: he waited until the last moment to do his work.

At the beginning of the semester, he promised himself that he would change. He bought a planner, downloaded productivity apps, and told his classmates that this time he would be more responsible. But every week, he repeated the same pattern. He delayed his readings, ignored small assignments, and studied only when exams were dangerously close.

One night, Leo had three tasks due the next morning. He tried to finish everything at once, but his mind was tired. He read the same paragraph five times without understanding it. He wrote sentences that did not make sense. He drank coffee, but his body wanted rest.

At that moment, he realized something important: procrastination had not saved him time; it had stolen his peace. After that experience, Leo decided to change in a realistic way. He did not try to become perfect overnight. Instead, he started using small strategies. He divided large assignments into smaller parts.

He studied for twenty-five minutes and rested for five. He wrote his tasks in order of importance. He also learned to start even when he did not feel motivated. Little by little, his stress decreased, and his confidence grew.
